title: Why Use Lindel?
description: Lindel — *linearization with delight* — encodes multi-dimensional integer points to a single integer along a [Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_curve) or [Morton (Z-order)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-order_curve) space-filling curve. Use it as the `ORDER BY` key when writing Parquet: multi-column range queries start skipping row groups, and bit-locality lets the file compress better.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: Sorting Parquet by a single column gives the reader tight per-row-group statistics on that one column — every other column ends up scattered. A space-filling curve gives you a single sort key that keeps neighbours close in *every* input dimension at once.

bulletPoints.label: Locality-sensitive sort keys
bulletPoints.description: `hilbert_encode` / `morton_encode` take an array of unsigned integers and return one sortable integer. Sort by it and points that were close in N dimensions are close in the file.

bulletPoints.label: Better Parquet block skipping
bulletPoints.description: Parquet stores per-row-group min/max statistics. With a Hilbert / Morton sort, every input column gets tight per-row-group bounds, so multi-column predicates each contribute to skipping instead of just the first sort column.

bulletPoints.label: Better compression
bulletPoints.description: Adjacent rows have adjacent coordinates, so RLE / dictionary / delta encodings inside each row group find more runs and shorter deltas. Files shrink, scans get faster.

bulletPoints.label: Round-trippable
bulletPoints.description: `hilbert_decode` / `morton_decode` recover the original array — useful for sanity checks and for storing the encoded value as a single-column index.

sections.title: Hilbert vs Morton
sections.description: Both curves are *locality-preserving* but they trade differently. Pick Hilbert by default; pick Morton when encoding throughput is the bottleneck.

bulletPoints.label: Hilbert — better locality
bulletPoints.description: The [Hilbert curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_curve) never makes long jumps in input space — neighbours along the curve are always neighbours in N-D. Tighter row-group bounding boxes, slightly more CPU to compute. The geometry indexing systems [S2](https://s2geometry.io/) (Google) and [H3](https://h3geo.org/) (Uber) use Hilbert-style ordering for the same reason.

bulletPoints.label: Morton — faster, simpler
bulletPoints.description: The [Morton / Z-order curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-order_curve) is just bit-interleaving the input dimensions. Trivially cheap to compute, with occasional long jumps at quadrant boundaries. The [Bing Maps Tile System](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/bingmaps/articles/bing-maps-tile-system) uses Morton-style quadkeys, and Delta Lake's original `ZORDER BY` was Morton before it moved to Hilbert-based [liquid clustering](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/clustering).

bulletPoints.label: Type coverage
bulletPoints.description: Both encoders are polymorphic over `UTINYINT` through `UHUGEINT`. Output is the smallest unsigned integer that fits *bit-width × dimensions* — e.g. `[UINTEGER, UINTEGER]` (32 × 2 = 64 bits) returns `UBIGINT`.

sections.title: What to know before you sort by it
sections.description: A few honest caveats so you pick the right tool and the right inputs.

bulletPoints.label: Inputs are unsigned integers
bulletPoints.description: Encode floats by quantizing first (`(lat * 1e6)::UINTEGER`) or by mapping signed ranges to unsigned. The curves only carry the bits they're given — pre-scale so meaningful precision lands in the high bits.

bulletPoints.label: Skewed dimensions
bulletPoints.description: If one input column has much higher cardinality than the others, the encoded ordering is dominated by it. Either rescale the dimensions to comparable ranges before encoding, or drop the dominant column from the curve and add it as a secondary sort key.

bulletPoints.label: Decoding doesn't carry types
bulletPoints.description: `hilbert_decode` / `morton_decode` need `num_elements`, `return_float`, and `return_unsigned` to reconstruct the original array — those aren't stored in the encoded integer.

bulletPoints.label: It's a write-time sort, not a magic index
bulletPoints.description: Lindel improves Parquet block skipping when files are written in encoded order. Updating Parquet later means rewriting; for streaming inserts, batch and re-sort on a cadence rather than hoping one row at a time will help.

useCases.title: Spatial Parquet — `(lat, lon)` or `(x, y, z)`
useCases.description: Hilbert-order points before writing. Bounding-box queries (`WHERE lat BETWEEN ... AND lon BETWEEN ...`) skip whole row groups they don't intersect. The same shape works for any geometry workload that lands in Parquet.

useCases.title: Time-series with categorical fanout — `(ts, symbol_id)` / `(ts, user_id)`
useCases.description: Sorting by `ts` alone scatters per-symbol rows. A Morton or Hilbert encoding of `(ts, key)` keeps both predicates skip-friendly.

useCases.title: Multi-column dashboards on a wide fact table
useCases.description: Pick the 2-4 columns that show up in `WHERE` together most often, encode them with `hilbert_encode`, and rewrite the Parquet ordered by that key. Same data, much better tail latency on filtered scans.

useCases.title: Compress better, transfer less
useCases.description: Bit-locality in the sort order means RLE / dictionary / delta encodings find more runs inside each row group. Smaller files at rest and on the wire.
